_population_not_person_comment: THIS DESCRIBES ~30 PEOPLE, NOT ONE, and that is the substantive difference from config/persona.json. Everything below is written at the level of the SHARED FLOOR -- entry-level, AI-adjacent, NYC or remote, no degree required (MASTER-PLAN-pursuit.md:41-42, 13-cohort-criteria-profile.md:25-33) -- because the plan is explicit that Builders are at different stages under a hands-off curriculum and that 'anything narrower is invented'. Where a real per-Builder difference exists (how much code someone writes, what they did before), the prose says so rather than picking one and pretending it is the cohort. background_summary: This profile scores postings for a cohort of roughly 30 Pursuit AI-Native Builders in New York City -- not for one candidate. They are early-career and career-changing adults completing an intensive, hands-off program in applied AI: using LLM tools fluently (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini), prompt design, workflow and process automation (Zapier, n8n, scripting), and building working things with AI assistance rather than studying AI theory. Most are seeking their first role in this field. Many bring substantial prior work experience from other industries -- healthcare, education, retail, hospitality, logistics, administration, the trades, the military -- and that experience is real seniority in its own domain and no seniority at all in this one. Most do not hold a computer science degree and some hold no degree; the program is the credential, and it is a new one that employers have not heard of. They are looking for entry-level, AI-adjacent work across ALL industries in the NYC metro, or remote work reachable from it. There is no single target role and inventing one would be wrong: the well-defined shared floor is entry-level, AI-adjacent, NYC or remote, and no degree required.
strengths: Fluent, daily, practical use of current AI tools -- not awareness of them. The distinguishing question is 'do you use these to do work' rather than 'can you explain a transformer', and for this cohort the answer is yes. Most incumbents in the operations, support, coordination and administrative roles these Builders are aiming at cannot say the same.

Automating real work: taking a manual process someone does by hand every week and turning it into a prompt, a script, a Zapier or n8n flow, or a documented AI-assisted procedure. This is the concrete, demonstrable version of 'AI-adjacent' and it maps onto ops, support, implementation and internal-systems work directly.

Substantial prior professional experience in another industry, for most of the cohort. Domain knowledge in healthcare, education, logistics, retail or public service plus AI-tool fluency is a genuinely uncommon combination, and it is worth most in exactly the non-tech NYC employers who are furthest from hiring a traditional engineer.

Adult-learner discipline. The curriculum is hands-off, so getting through it required self-direction, working without a syllabus, and finishing projects nobody was checking on -- which is the behaviour the job actually needs and the thing a degree does not evidence.

Comfortable enough with technical work to be useful beside engineers: reading and modifying scripts, working with APIs and spreadsheets and data, writing clear documentation. The strength here is being technical enough to bridge, not being a software engineer.
honest_gaps: No professional experience in an AI-adjacent role, for most of the cohort. A posting asking for two or more years of specific AI, ML, data or software experience is a stretch at best, and one asking for three or more is out of reach regardless of how strong the transferable story is.

Prior seniority does not transfer. A Builder may have fifteen years and a management title in nursing or logistics and still be entry-level here. A posting that wants an experienced individual contributor in THIS domain is a mismatch even when the person is far from junior in general -- and the posting's stated seniority describes the posting, never the person.

No graduate degree, frequently no computer science degree, and some without a bachelor's. Any posting that genuinely requires an advanced degree is disqualifying, and this is a defining constraint of the population rather than a preference.
No machine learning research or model-training background at all. Roles wanting research, deep ML theory, model architecture or training infrastructure are the wrong roles, not merely hard ones.

Software engineering depth varies widely across the cohort and cannot be assumed. Some Builders can hold a junior developer role; many cannot. Treat a coding-heavy posting as a possible fit for part of the cohort rather than a fit or a miss for all of it.

The credential is unfamiliar. Pursuit's AI-Native program is new, so a hiring manager screening on brand-name school or employer will not recognise it, and postings that lean on pedigree are a poor use of anyone's application.
Geographically constrained. The cohort is in New York City and largely needs to be in or near it; a remote role is fine and an onsite role in another metro is not.
scoring_instructions: Score fit_score 0-100 for how well this posting fits a typical member of this cohort -- an entry-level, AI-fluent career changer in NYC with no degree requirement met and no prior experience in this field. Do not inflate. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SIGNAL is whether the role wants someone who USES AI tools to do the work -- prompting, automating, evaluating output, building simple workflows -- rather than someone who BUILDS AI systems. A posting that expects fluency with ChatGPT or Claude in an operations, support, implementation, coordination, marketing, internal-systems or administrative role is the target and should score high; a posting that wants LLM features shipped into a production codebase is a real but harder stretch and should score moderately; a posting requiring ML research, a graduate degree, or several years of engineering is a poor fit however AI-heavy it sounds. WEIGHT THE STATED REQUIREMENTS, NOT THE INDUSTRY. All industries are in scope, and a hospital, school district, city agency, law firm, logistics company or retailer is as good a destination as a technology company -- often better, because the AI-tool fluency is scarcer there. Score an entry-level posting at a non-tech NYC employer on its own merits and do not discount it for being unglamorous. gap_bridging_angle is where the transferable-experience story belongs and it must be specific to THIS posting: name the prior-industry experience or the AI-tool skill that this employer would actually care about, in one or two concrete sentences, and never write generic career-change advice. It is also the right place to note when substantial prior seniority in another field is an asset here, which is a thing the numeric weights deliberately cannot represent. risk_factors should flag what would genuinely sink an application: a stated experience minimum above about two years, a required degree, an onsite requirement outside the NYC metro, a security clearance, a licence or certification the cohort does not hold, or an AI mention that turns out to be company boilerplate rather than part of the job. Say when the posting's AI language is decorative -- that is the most common failure mode in this corpus and naming it is more useful than a score.
